thread.title: Will robots, AI and self-driving cars take your job: See who and where will get hit hardest

author: Mike Sunnucks
title: Will robots, AI and self-driving cars take your job: See who and where will get hit hardest
text: – Senior Reporter, Phoenix Business Journal Jan 24, 2018, 2:49pm MST Subhash Kak says he isn’t anti-technology. He is a computer science professor at Oklahoma State University. “I work on AI myself,” he said. “I know things have to progress.” But Kak also says the world (and workforce) will be in for some massive changes if self-driving cars, artificial intelligence and robots are widely adopted and put to use. That could mean millions of workers put out of jobs by technology and others needed to be retrained. While technology advances bring the promise of productivity gains and reducing human error, they also run the risk of leaving lower skilled and other workers behind, Kak said. A recent study by McKinsey Co. estimates between 400 million and 800 million workers worldwide could be displaced by automation. Is your job and industry one of them? We take a look at several industries and arenas where Kak and others say robots, AI and autonomous cars and trucks will not only cause major disruptions but could also eliminate jobs and the need for workers and even physical locations. • Transportation and logistics Self-driving cars are being tested at a fast pace with the likes of Uber, General Motors (NYSE: GM) and Alphabet (Nasdaq: GOOGL) offshoot Waymo all doing that in Arizona. They are in a race with other automakers including Elon Musk’s Tesla Inc. (Nasdaq: TSLA) and Volkswagen to hit the roads with just a computer behind the wheel. When that day comes then autonomous trucks are just around the corner and that could eliminate millions of jobs for drivers and others in the trucking and logistics sectors. “If self-driving cars and trucks get to be adopted widely certainly that will have a major impact,” Kak said. “A large section of the population is in transportation.” Kak said the changes resulting from self-driving cars and trucks could be on par with changes to transport networks from railroads. That means changed employment and career landscape for delivery drivers, big logistics companies such as United Parcel Service (NYSE: UPS) and FedEx (NYSE: FDX), big trucking companies such as Knight Transportation (NYSE: KNX) and Swift Transportation (NYSE: SWFT) and their workers. Knight and Swift are both based in Phoenix and merging. UPS is developing a next generation, automation-heavy, e-commerce focused regional center in Goodyear. • Retail and restaurants Amazon.com Inc. (Nasdaq: AMZN) just opened a grocery market in Seattle without cashiers or checkout lanes. Smartphone and other technologies charge customers for what they grab. Amazon also has some automation heavy distribution centers in its vast logistic network. Restaurants from Panera Bread and Carl’s Jr. (NYSE: CKR) to Jack in the Box (Nasdaq: JACK), McDonald’s (NYSE: MCD) and KFC and Taco Bell owner Yum! Brands (NYSE: YUM) have or are moving toward adopting more automation in their restaurants and operations. Retailers and grocers such as Target (NYSE: TGT) and Wal-Mart Stores (Nasdaq: WMT) and Kroger (NYSE: KR) have already installed more automated self-checkouts. That is usually accompanied by a cut in staffing. Walmart bought e-commerce site Jet.com and Kroger could buy Overstock.com (Nasdaq: OSTK). Those are aimed at keeping up with Amazon. But they also are part of a technology wave across the sector. Eric Schiffer, CEO of Patriarch Equity, said department stores and retailers such as Macy’s need to up their e-commerce and digital games — and fast — to keep up with Amazon. Schiffer also said traditional stores need to adopt automation and technology that makes their customer service and store experience more like what consumers get when go online with customized and personalized searches and recommendations. • Women, immigrants and working class Technological changes and potential worker displacements have wider impacts than just in retail stores and restaurants. Many of those workers have lower or entry level skill sets, don’t make great wages and often have lower education levels. If those types of workers are put out of work, economies run the risk of a new permanent underclass and great income disparities. Arizona has a 17.5 percent poverty rate when income as well as living expenses are taken into account, according to the U.S. Census Bureau. In California, that poverty rate is 20.6 percent — the highest in the U.S. The poverty rate for Hispanics is 25.4 percent, It is 23.4 percent for African Americans, 28.7 percent for female-headed households and 29.1 percent for undocumented immigrants. All that comes as the stock market has gained $6.9 trillion in value since President Donald Trump took office, according to CNBC. The Dow Jones Industrial Average has zoomed past 26,000 this year. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq are also on record streaks. But most of those stock windfalls are going to the super rich. British charity Oxfam estimates the top percent took in 82 percent of the wealth gained last year. A new report by the World Economic Forum found women could be more negatively impact than men by automation. That’s because women are working in positions — such as administrative, food service and other jobs — more likely to be impacted by automation. Kak said that automation could also reduce the need for immigrant labor in the U.S. • Manufacturing and construction The manufacturing and construction sectors are adopting automation and robotics at a brisk pace. That could impact everything from manufacturing plants in China to construction sites in Phoenix, Los Angeles and other U.S. cities. Dan Kara, research director for robotics at ABI Research told the Association of Equipment Manufacturers , said AI in construction is limited now. “But it is growing, particularly in applications involving machine vision for surveying and analyzing materials and structures, or for robotics applications such as automated bricklaying or autonomous vehicles.” Kara said. That comes for a U.S. construction industry that is already short on workers especially craftsman and truck drivers. • Anywhere and everywhere McKinsey estimates half of all jobs in China would be impacted significantly by automation. Scores of U.S. companies from Apple Inc . (Nasdaq: AAPL) to Nike (NYSE: NKE) have big manufacturing footprints in China and Asia. In India and Mexico, 52 percent of jobs could be impacted while 46 percent of U.S. jobs could face big changes from automation, according to McKinsey. That parallels an Oxford University estimate that 47 percent of Americans jobs will disrupted or changed because of automation. • Colleges and schools Kak said one of the biggest and perhaps least expected changes that looks to come from AI and automation will be in education — espeically higher education. The Oklahoma State University professor sees as many as half of existing colleges and universities potentially closing. He points to colleges closing in India. Kak said colleges sprouted centuries ago around libraries. Now, everyone has a library at their fingertips on their iPhones. Colleges and higher education has already been migrating online — a model pioneered by University of Phoenix and now adopted by ASU, Liberty University, the University of Massachusetts , University of Maryland and Grand Canyon University. Like with self-driving cars, Arizona has been a hub for online education via ASU and its for-profit counterparts UOP and GCU (Nasdaq: LOPE). • Media and news While Trump decries his media critics as biased and ‘fake news,’ the industry is struggling with the decline in print and an ability to monetize digital content. Artificial intelligence and automation could continue to dramatically change the media landscape just as internet and then social media and search engine giants (i.e. Facebook (NYSE: FB), Twitter (NYSE: TWTR) and Google / Alphabet (Nasdaq: GOOGL)) have. Media companies that leverage the technology to better track, market and personalize news will have a better chance at survival. – Senior Reporter, Phoenix Business Journal Jan 24, 2018, 2:49pm MST
